description: The workflow engine's altinn.workflow_engine.* OpenTelemetry metrics: health, workflow lifecycle, latency, resources, mailboxes and throttling.

panels.description: Engine self-assessed health, the worst across the selected instances: 0=Healthy, 1=Degraded, 2=Unhealthy. No data means no engine instance is reporting; see Instances.
panels.title: Engine Health

panels.description: Engine processes reporting metrics, counted from altinn.workflow_engine.health.status, which every engine process exports. Zero means no engine in the selected services is reporting. A restarted process reports under a new service.instance.id, so the process it replaced can count for a short while after it stopped.
panels.title: Instances

panels.description: All failure signals: errors broken down by subsystem, workflow failures by reason, plus step/DB failures and the consecutive maintenance failure count of the worst instance (right axis).
panels.title: Failures

panels.description: Inbox queue utilization. At 100% the engine activates backpressure and rejects new work (429). Every replica reports the same database-wide count, so replicas are combined with max() rather than sum().
panels.title: Queue Fill

panels.description: Successful workflow completions per second
panels.title: Throughput

panels.description: Total retry events per second: every step retry plus every shutdown-driven workflow requeue. Step retries already imply a workflow requeue with reason=step_retry, so that path is counted once via the step counter only.
panels.title: Retries

panels.description: Percentage of completed workflows that succeeded
panels.title: Success Rate

panels.description: 95th percentile workflow duration for a single attempt (queue + processing). Retries land as separate samples.
panels.title: P95 Duration

panels.description: Rate of incoming workflow write requests vs accepted, plus read-side query traffic
panels.title: Workflow Requests

panels.description: Rate of workflow lifecycle events. Failed/Canceled/Requeued broken down by reason — failed: execution / dependency_failed / poisoned / wait_expired (a step's wait budget ran out) / manual (a caller failed a parked workflow through the fail endpoint); canceled: before_processing / during_processing; requeued: step_retry / shutdown.
panels.title: Workflow Outcomes

panels.description: Current workflow counts by state (gauge values over time). Finished = all terminal (success + failed + canceled + dep-failed). Every replica reports the same database-wide counts, so replicas are combined with max() and only separate services, each with its own database, are added up.
panels.title: Workflow Inventory

panels.description: Rate of durable yields. A deferral is a command reporting “ran fine, the awaited outcome is not available yet” — it is not a failure and does not consume a retry. Step deferrals exceed workflow deferrals whenever one workflow parks repeatedly. Wait Budget Expired is the failure mode this row is here to make visible: a step that kept deferring until its waitBudget ran out, failed with reason=wait_expired — deliberately excluded from the default ops alert, so this is where it surfaces.
panels.title: Deferrals

panels.description: Workflows currently parked in Waiting because a step deferred. Waiting is in the Incomplete/active set — no lease, no worker slot, no backoff timer of its own — so this population is invisible in the Active/Scheduled gauges on the Workflow Inventory panel. A level that only ever rises means deferring commands are never resolving. Every replica reports the same database-wide count, so replicas are combined with max() rather than sum().
panels.title: Waiting Workflows

panels.description: Percentiles of the wait budget a deferring step actually consumed, from its first deferral to the moment it resolved — completed, expired, or failed. Recorded once per deferring step, so a step that deferred forty times contributes one sample. Compare the upper percentiles against the configured command.waitBudget (default 24h): this is the only signal that shows budgets being approached rather than blown.
panels.title: Wait Budget Consumed (per deferring step)

panels.description: Namespace circuit breakers currently in the Tripped state. Zero is the normal reading. The gauge carries no namespace label — it is a per-process scalar — and every replica reports its own snapshot of the same shared state table, so replicas are combined with max() rather than sum(). The feature ships dark: with EngineSettings:Throttling:Enabled left false the sweep never runs and this stays flat at zero. workflow-engine-app turns it on; the engine's own test host only does with the playground compose override.
panels.title: Breakers Tripped

panels.description: Circuit-breaker state changes in the last 5 minutes, per namespace. These are rare discrete events, so this is increase() rather than the rate() the throughput panels use — one trip reads as 1, not as 0.003/s. Tripped includes re-trips from a failed recovery. Extended means every canary failed its probe and the throttle window doubled. Cleared means recovery drained the parked population. Handler Parked counts workflows the handler parked the moment they failed retryably in an already-tripped namespace — the sweep's own parking is not counted there, so this series stays flat when the storm is not producing fresh failures.
panels.title: Breaker Transitions by Namespace

panels.description: Rate at which recovery cohorts hand parked workflows back to the fetch gate, per namespace. Counted by the number of rows actually released, not once per cohort, and cohorts double every sweep — so a healthy recovery is a rising curve that stops abruptly when the last cohort comes back empty and the breaker clears. This is the only throttle counter with a population large enough to read as a rate.
panels.title: Workflows Released from Throttling by Namespace

panels.description: Workflow duration percentiles for a single attempt (queue + processing). Retries land as separate samples; see Outcomes for retry rate.
panels.title: Workflow Duration (per attempt)

panels.description: Per-attempt P95 of queue wait and active execution, stacked. Stack height is the sum of two marginal P95s — useful for seeing where tail latency is concentrated, but it does not reconcile arithmetically with the Workflow Duration panel's P95(total) because percentiles are not additive across the queue/processing decomposition. Within a single attempt, queue + processing does equal total by construction.
panels.title: Workflow Time Breakdown (P95, per attempt)

panels.description: Step duration percentiles for a single attempt (queue + processing). Step retries land as separate samples — see Step Failures for retry rate.
panels.title: Step Duration (per attempt)

panels.description: Per-attempt P95 of step queue wait (engine/DB overhead between steps) and active execution, stacked. Stack height is the sum of two marginal P95s — useful for seeing whether queue or processing drives tail latency, but it does not reconcile arithmetically with the Step Duration panel's P95(total) because percentiles are not additive across the queue/processing decomposition. Within a single attempt, queue + processing does equal total by construction.
panels.title: Step Time Breakdown (P95, per attempt)

panels.description: Worker concurrency slots: used vs total capacity
panels.title: Worker Slots

panels.description: Database operation concurrency slots: used vs total capacity
panels.title: DB Slots

panels.description: HTTP call concurrency slots: used vs total capacity
panels.title: HTTP Slots

panels.description: Inbox slots: active workflows against the backpressure threshold, used vs total capacity. Both are derived from the database-wide active workflow count, which every replica reports identically, so replicas are combined with max() rather than sum().
panels.title: Inbox Slots

panels.description: Processing loop iterations per minute
panels.title: Main Loop Rate

panels.description: P95 of each main-loop iteration broken down: Queue (post-fetch wait — debounce or ~500ms idle ceiling) and Active Work (fetch + dispatch), stacked. Total is the joint P95 of the same iterations, drawn outside the stack: percentiles are not additive, so it will not equal the stack height, and the gap between them is exactly how much that non-additivity costs you here. For iteration throughput see Main Loop Rate.
panels.title: Main Loop Time (P95)

panels.description: Rate of database operations by outcome
panels.title: Database Operations

panels.description: Update buffer throughput: total submitted (deduped + flushed), items flushed to DB, and items eliminated by deduplication
panels.title: Update Buffer Throughput

panels.description: Receive workflows the rendezvous could not answer for — tagged unregistered or undecided. Both mean the engine is violating an invariant of its own rendezvous, which is why they fail the step critically rather than retryably: a retry would launder the violation. ALERT ON ANY VALUE ABOVE ZERO; this is a different pager from a step failing because the app returned an error. The `or vector(0)` keeps the panel reading a true zero rather than “No data” before the counter has ever fired.
panels.title: Rendezvous Violations

panels.description: Mailboxes still open more than one MailboxSweepInterval past their deadline. Exactly zero is the only healthy reading — anything else means the deadline sweep is not running or not draining. A mass timeout can make it briefly non-zero while one tick drains, so alert on persistence rather than on a single sample. The count saturates at 10 000, so never read it as an exact backlog size. Every replica reports the same database-wide count, so replicas are combined with max() rather than sum().
panels.title: Overdue Open Mailboxes

panels.description: Accepted deliveries that no receiver was ever enqueued for, counted when a mailbox closes at its deadline. Not an engine fault — the message was accepted and stored exactly as promised — but it means a saga stopped reading before the other side stopped writing, so the reply was never consumed. Non-zero deserves a look at the owning app, not a page.
panels.title: Unpaired Deliveries

panels.description: Mints and closures per second. Minted excludes idempotent replays, which create nothing. Closures are split by reason: `request` is a DELETE from the owning saga (the healthy path), `deadline` is the sweep closing a mailbox nobody came back for. A `deadline` share that climbs means sagas are abandoning exchanges rather than finishing them.
panels.title: Mailbox Lifecycle

panels.description: Every delivery request the engine answered, by verdict. `accepted` appended a message; `duplicate` replayed a stored idempotency key and is a healthy forwarder retrying, not an error. The refusals — `closed`, `not_found`, `log_full`, `too_large`, `invalid` — store nothing, so their keys stay free for a corrected replay. Note that the idempotency lookup runs before the refusals, so a kept message still replays 200 after the mailbox closed.
panels.title: Deliveries by Outcome

panels.description: Receive workflows entering and leaving the rendezvous. Every receiver registers, not only the parked ones. Births, by how the receiver was born: `held` is born waiting for a message that has not arrived, `delivered` is born already holding one, `closed` is born into a mailbox that had already closed. Releases, by cause: `delivered` is a message arriving for a parked receiver, `closed` is closure releasing every receiver at once. `held` births and total releases should track each other over time; a persistent gap is receivers that never got woken.
panels.title: Receivers: Births & Releases

panels.description: Percentiles of the gap between a parked receiver being released and a worker first claiming it. NOTIFY is issued inside the releasing transaction and the processor debounces it by 10ms, so the healthy population is tens of milliseconds; a release whose NOTIFY was missed is claimed on the next fetch cycle, which puts a soft ceiling around the 500ms idle poll. Anything materially above that is worker starvation, not mailbox latency. Values are clamped at zero because the two ends come from two pods' clocks.
panels.title: Receiver Wake Latency

panels.description: The one thing the engine emits that answers “is mailbox batching actually happening?” — requests answered by a flush divided by flushes, per operation, over the same window. Both counters are recorded at the same point once a batch is known answered, so a faulted flush counts in neither. 1.0 means every request flushed alone, and for deliveries that is worse than the bespoke path it replaced: the break-even is a mean batch of about 1.25 (the batched delivery flush issues a fixed five statements). The ceiling is MaxBatchSize, 100 for all three buffers; a ratio pinned there means the buffer is saturated and that setting is what to tune next. altinn.workflow_engine.mailbox_buffer.depth cannot answer this question — see the Buffer Depth panel.
panels.title: Mean Batch Size (flushed ÷ batches)

panels.description: Mailbox requests waiting for a batch flush, per operation. Read this as LATENCY, not capacity: the queues wait rather than refuse when full, so a sustained depth means callers waiting longer for a verdict, never requests turned away. Read only the sustained value — it is a 5s sample of a queue that fills and drains between flushes, and a storm accepting 3.86 messages per flush held it at zero throughout. A zero here is therefore no evidence the queue never filled, and this panel cannot tell you whether batching is happening. Mean Batch Size is what does.
panels.title: Buffer Depth

panels.description: Rate of step executions by outcome
panels.title: Step Execution

panels.description: Error rate broken down by subsystem (workflow_processing / fetch_and_lock / db_maintenance / metrics_collector / throttle_sweep / mailbox_deadline_close / mailbox_deadline_sweep) plus stale-workflow reclaim rate.
panels.title: Errors & Recovery

panels.description: Npgsql connection pool: idle vs active connections. Stacked area shows total pool usage over time. These are Npgsql's standard db.client.* metrics, which the metric allowlist in Altinn's environments drops (only altinn.*, http.* and signalr.server.* pass), so this row shows data only locally.
panels.title: Pool Utilization

panels.description: Npgsql connection creation time and command execution duration. High create time = network/PG issue. High command duration = slow queries. These are Npgsql's standard db.client.* metrics, which the metric allowlist in Altinn's environments drops (only altinn.*, http.* and signalr.server.* pass), so this row shows data only locally.
panels.title: Latency (P95 / P50)

panels.description: Currently executing commands, total open connections, and pool max boundary. Executing near pool limit = saturation. These are Npgsql's standard db.client.* metrics, which the metric allowlist in Altinn's environments drops (only altinn.*, http.* and signalr.server.* pass), so this row shows data only locally.
panels.title: Connections & Pool Limits

panels.description: Rate of in-flight workflows abandoned because the row's lease token no longer matches at write-back. Non-zero indicates heartbeat lag or aggressive maintenance reclaim — workflows self-heal via reclaim, but downstream side effects may have been duplicated.
panels.title: Lease Lost

panels.description: Rate of fetched workflows skipped because they were already in-flight on this host — same-host DbMaintenance reclaim raced the main fetch loop. Self-heals on the next maintenance sweep.
panels.title: Fetch Race Dropped

panels.description: Rate of fire-and-forget status updates dropped because the update-buffer channel was full. These are real losses (intermediate progress updates) — non-zero signals backpressure exceeding the buffer's capacity.
panels.title: Update Buffer Dropped

panels.description: Operator actions on workflows the engine had already placed, in the last 5 minutes. Discrete and rare, so increase() rather than rate(). Nudged cleared a parked workflow's backoff so it runs on the next fetch cycle instead of when its timer elapses — the engine's push channel, an acceleration that is never load-bearing for correctness. Abandoned wrote off an unsuccessful terminal workflow, which stops it condemning dependents evaluated afterwards and atomically releases its enqueue idempotency key, so replaying the same fingerprint creates a fresh workflow instead of deduplicating onto the write-off.
panels.title: Operator Interventions

panels.description: DependencyFailed workflows re-enqueued in the last 5 minutes because their dependencies have all completed since — the engine healing itself, and the only counter on this row nobody triggered by hand. The maintenance sweep that does it runs once a minute, so this lags its cause. On its own panel rather than beside the interventions because abandonments outrun recoveries by two orders of magnitude and would flatten this to the baseline.
panels.title: Dependency Recovery

list.description: The deployment.environment.name of the engines. Locally it is always local.
list.label: Environment
list.name: env

list.description: The engine services to show. All is every engine service reporting in the environment rather than any service, so the Npgsql panels leave out other services' connection pools.
list.label: Service
list.name: service
